topics.title: energy bands
topics.essence: In a crystal an electron's energy can only lie in allowed bands. In a semiconductor the valence band is full and the conduction band empty, with a gap E_g between (1.12 eV in silicon). Only electrons lifted across the gap, and their holes, carry current.
topics.check: Why does a perfectly pure silicon crystal at 0 K carry no current at all, even with a field across it?

topics.title: electrons and holes
topics.essence: Break one bond and you get two carriers: a free electron, and a vacancy that neighbouring electrons hop into, so the vacancy moves like a positive particle. The hole is the bookkeeping for a band that is almost full.
topics.check: A field points to the right inside a piece of silicon. Which way do the electrons drift, which way do the holes drift, and which way does each one's current point?

topics.title: intrinsic carriers
topics.essence: In pure silicon every free electron leaves a hole, so n = p = n_i, about 10¹⁰ cm⁻³ at 300 K. Heat lifts more electrons across the gap, so n_i grows exponentially with temperature: roughly doubling every 9 K near room temperature.
topics.check: Why does a semiconductor conduct better when it is heated, while a metal conducts worse?

topics.title: mass-action law
topics.essence: Generation and recombination balance in equilibrium, so the product np stays at n_i² whatever the doping. Push n up a millionfold with donors and p falls a millionfold.
topics.check: Silicon is doped with 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ donors. How many holes per cm³ are there at 300 K, and why are there fewer than in pure silicon?

topics.title: doping
topics.essence: Phosphorus has one electron more than its four bonds need and gives it away; boron has one fewer and takes one, leaving a hole. A few dopant atoms per million set which carrier dominates. With both kinds present, the larger wins by the difference.
topics.check: Silicon holds 10¹⁷ cm⁻³ boron and 4×10¹⁶ cm⁻³ phosphorus. Is it n-type or p-type, and roughly how many majority carriers per cm³ does it have?

topics.title: potential and doping
topics.essence: A doped region's potential, measured from intrinsic silicon, is (kT/q)·ln(n/n_i): about 60 mV per decade of doping, positive for n-type and negative for p-type. Every built-in potential is a difference of two of these.
topics.check: An n-type region has 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ electrons and n_i = 10¹⁰ cm⁻³. Without a calculator, what is its potential relative to intrinsic silicon?

topics.title: mobility
topics.essence: A carrier is pushed by the field, then knocked off course by a collision about every tenth of a picosecond. Mobility μ is its average drift speed per unit field. Dopant ions and a hotter lattice scatter more and lower μ. Electrons outrun holes 2 to 3 times.
topics.check: You raise the doping of a silicon bar tenfold. Why does its resistivity fall by less than ten times?

topics.title: drift current
topics.essence: A field adds a small average velocity v = μE on top of fast random motion. Current density is charge times density times that velocity, J = q(nμ_n + pμ_p)E. Electrons and holes drift opposite ways, but both currents point along E.
topics.check: Two bars of the same size carry the same current. One has twice the electron density. How does its electron drift velocity compare with the other's?

topics.title: resistivity
topics.essence: A doped bar's resistivity is set almost entirely by its majority carriers: ρ ≈ 1/(qNμ) for a doping N. The minority carriers are outnumbered by many decades and add nothing you could measure.
topics.check: A bar is doped with 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ donors. Why can you ignore its holes when you work out its resistance, even though they drift too?

topics.title: diffusion current
topics.essence: Random motion alone carries particles from where they are crowded to where they are sparse, with no field at all. The flow follows the slope of the concentration: J_n = qD_n·dn/dx for electrons and J_p = −qD_p·dp/dx for holes.
topics.check: Holes are piled up at the left end of a bar and spread to the right. Which way does the hole current point? Which way would the current point if electrons were piled up there instead?

topics.title: Einstein relation
topics.essence: Drift and diffusion are both limited by the same collisions, so the diffusion constant and the mobility are tied: D/μ = kT/q. Know how mobile a carrier is and you know how fast it spreads.
topics.check: Electrons in a sample have a mobility of 1000 cm²/V·s. What is their diffusion constant at 300 K, and why should cooling the sample change the ratio D/μ?

topics.title: velocity saturation
topics.essence: At high fields carriers lose energy to the lattice as fast as the field gives it, so their drift speed stops near 10⁷ cm/s in silicon. A very short transistor then carries a current that grows linearly with V_GS − V_T instead of as its square.
topics.check: A transistor's channel is made ten times shorter, at the same voltages. Why does its current grow by much less than ten times?

topics.title: recombination and lifetime
topics.essence: An extra electron in p-type silicon survives, on average, a lifetime τ before it meets a hole and recombines, usually at a defect near the middle of the gap. Disturb the balance and the excess dies away as e^(−t/τ).
topics.check: Light makes extra electrons and holes in a p-type bar and is then switched off. What sets how fast the extra electrons disappear, and why does the hole density barely change in relative terms?

links.why: Each broken bond makes one electron and one hole, which is why n = p in pure silicon.
The gap E_g is the energy each pair must be given, so a wider gap means exponentially fewer carriers.
The share of electrons lifted across the gap is a Boltzmann factor, which is where the exponential in temperature comes from.
An empty state in a nearly full valence band is what moves as a hole.
Pure silicon fixes the product: np = n_i·n_i, and doping changes the split but not the product.
Doping sets the majority density, and np = n_i² then fixes the minority density.
A donor adds electrons without holes and an acceptor adds holes without electrons.
Carrier density follows potential as a Boltzmann factor, so potential follows the logarithm of density.
The doping sets n or p, and the log of its ratio to n_i sets the potential.
Ionized dopants are charged obstacles, so more doping means more scattering and lower mobility.
Mobility turns a field into a drift velocity, v = μE.
J = σE is Ohm's law written per unit area and per unit length.
Resistivity is 1/σ, and σ = q(nμ_n + pμ_p) is the drift current per unit field.
np = n_i² makes the minority density so small that only the majority term in σ counts.
Both carriers spread down their own gradients, and their opposite charges set the signs of the two currents.
D measures how fast carriers spread, which is the quantity the relation ties to μ.
The same collision time sets both the drift speed per unit field and the spreading rate.
In equilibrium drift must cancel diffusion in a Boltzmann-shaped profile, and that forces D/μ = kT/q.
v = μE holds only at low fields; velocity saturation is where that straight line flattens.
Recombination is the process that pulls np back to n_i² after it is disturbed.
The excess decays at a rate proportional to itself, so it falls like any first-order system with time constant τ.
